title: What recruitment AI is (and is not)
description: A plain definition of recruitment AI, the four jobs it does today, and the marketing claims to ignore.
body:
Recruitment AI is software that performs a recruiting task that used to need a person's judgement: finding candidates, writing to them, reading applications, answering applicants, scheduling interviews, taking notes, or predicting who will succeed. The word covers everything from a chatbot that answers "is this role remote?" to an autonomous agent that sources and contacts a shortlist overnight.

It is useful to separate three things that get lumped together.

  • Automation follows rules a human wrote: "if the applicant lacks a driving licence, reject". It has been in applicant tracking systems for twenty years and involves no learning.
  • Machine learning finds patterns in past data: which résumés led to hires, which outreach got replies. It predicts; it does not understand.
  • Generative and agentic AI (large language models) read and write natural language and can plan multi-step work. This is what changed between 2022 and today, and it is why the term "recruitment AI" suddenly means something different.

The four jobs recruitment AI actually does

  1. Finding and contacting people (sourcing). AI searches profile databases and the open web, ranks people against a brief, finds contact details and writes outreach. The most advanced version is an AI sourcing agent that does the whole loop and returns replies.
  2. Reading and sorting applications (screening and matching). Models score how well an application matches a job, or ask knockout questions by chat.
  3. Talking to candidates (conversational AI). Chatbots and SMS assistants answer questions, collect information and book interviews, mostly in high-volume hourly hiring.
  4. Supporting interviews and decisions (interview intelligence). AI transcribes interviews, writes notes against a scorecard, and flags inconsistent questioning.

What it is not

It is not a robot that hires. Almost no organisation lets software make a final hiring decision, and in several jurisdictions doing so without human review is unlawful. It is also not, usually, a single product. Most companies run several narrow AI features inside tools they already own, plus one or two dedicated AI products for sourcing or screening.

Marketing to ignore. "AI-powered" on a product that parses résumés into fields, or that shows a dashboard, describes nothing new. Ask: which task does the AI complete that a person used to do, and how do you measure that it did it well?

faq.q: Is recruitment AI the same as an applicant tracking system?
faq.a: No. An applicant tracking system (ATS) stores candidates and moves them through stages. Recruitment AI performs tasks on top of that record: sourcing, screening, messaging, note-taking. Most ATSs now include some AI features, and many AI tools plug into an ATS.

faq.q: Is recruitment AI only for large companies?
faq.a: No. The newest category, autonomous sourcing agents, is most useful to small teams with no recruiter, and several products are priced as one flat team plan rather than per seat. Enterprise tools for high-volume screening remain expensive.

title: How recruitment AI works, without the jargon
description: Embeddings, ranking models, language models and agents explained with recruiting examples.
body:
You do not need to understand the mathematics, but four ideas explain almost every product.

1. Turning text into numbers (embeddings)

A model converts a résumé, a job description or a profile into a long list of numbers that captures its meaning. Two texts about similar work end up with similar numbers even if they share no keywords. This is why modern matching finds a "growth marketer" when you searched for "demand generation manager", and why Boolean strings are fading.

2. Ranking

Given a brief and a thousand candidates, a ranking model orders them by predicted fit. The prediction is trained on examples: past hires, recruiter shortlists, who replied, who advanced. The quality of a ranking depends entirely on what it was trained to predict. "Looks like people we hired before" is a different target from "will pass a structured interview", and the first one is where bias enters.

3. Large language models

Language models read and write. In recruiting they draft outreach, summarise interviews, answer candidate questions, extract requirements from a messy job description and explain why a candidate ranked where they did. They are strong at language and weak at facts they were not given; a well-built product keeps them grounded in your data.

4. Agents

An agent is a language model given tools (search, a contact database, an email account, a calendar) and a goal, and allowed to take several steps towards it. A sourcing agent, for example, reads a brief, runs searches across several sources, ranks the results, looks up and verifies contact details, writes a personalised message to each person, sends it by email or SMS, waits for replies and reports back. The human sets the brief and reviews the output; the agent does the hours in between.

Putting it together: one sourcing run

  1. Brief A recruiter writes two paragraphs: the role, must-haves, nice-to-haves, location, compensation range.
  2. Search The agent turns the brief into several searches and runs them across licensed profile data and the open web, gathering a few thousand possible people.
  3. Rank Each person is scored against the brief; the top few hundred are kept, with a reason for each.
  4. Verify contacts Email addresses and phone numbers are found and checked so messages are deliverable.
  5. Outreach A short, specific email (and, where appropriate, an SMS) is written for each person, referencing their actual work. Follow-ups are scheduled.
  6. Replies Interested people are handed to the recruiter or pushed into the ATS; the agent keeps a log of what it did and why.
What to take from this. The quality of recruitment AI is set by three things you can ask about: what data it searches, what the ranking was trained to predict, and how the language model is kept honest. Vendors who cannot answer those three questions are selling the label.

faq.q: Does recruitment AI learn from my company's data?
faq.a: Some products fine-tune on your past hiring data; most use general models plus your current brief. Ask whether your data trains models used for other customers, and whether you can opt out.

faq.q: What is the difference between a chatbot and an agent?
faq.a: A chatbot answers one message at a time within a script. An agent pursues a goal across many steps and tools (search, email, calendar) and decides what to do next; a human reviews the result rather than every step.

title: The seven types of recruitment AI
description: Sourcing agents, talent search, screening and matching, conversational AI, interview intelligence, scheduling, and writing assistants, with what each replaces.
body:
Products are easier to evaluate when you know which type you are looking at. Each type replaces a specific chunk of work.

TypeWhat it replacesWho buys itExamples
AI sourcing agentsThe sourcer's day: searching, ranking, finding contacts, writing and sending outreachStartups, lean talent teams, agenciesNoon
AI talent searchBoolean search across profile databases; contact findingEnterprise TA teams, agenciesSeekOut, hireEZ, LinkedIn Recruiter AI features
Screening and matchingReading and ranking applications; knockout questionsHigh-volume employers, large ATS usersEightfold, HireVue, ATS-native matching
Conversational AIAnswering applicants, collecting details, booking interviewsRetail, hospitality, healthcare, logisticsParadox, Sense
Interview intelligenceNote-taking, debrief summaries, interviewer coachingAny team with structured interviewsMetaview, BrightHire
Scheduling automationCoordinating panels across calendars and time zonesMid-market and enterpriseGoodTime, ATS schedulers
Writing and workflow assistantsDrafting job descriptions, emails, scorecards; summarising profilesEveryone, usually inside the ATSAshby AI, Greenhouse AI, Workable AI

AI sourcing agents

The newest and most autonomous type. You give the agent a role brief; it searches, ranks, verifies contact details, writes personalised messages and sends them by email and SMS, then returns the people who replied. The value is that the work happens whether or not anyone had time for it, which is why it suits teams without a dedicated sourcer. Judge an agent on reply rate, the relevance of the shortlist, and how transparent it is about why each person was chosen. Noon is the clearest example of the category.

AI talent search

Databases of hundreds of millions of profiles with AI-assisted search: paste a job description and get a ranked list, with filters LinkedIn lacks (code repositories, patents, clearances, diversity indicators). The human still runs the search and the outreach. Strong for specialist roles; expensive; requires a skilled user.

Screening and matching

Models score applications against the job and surface the best ones first, or ask structured knockout questions. This is the type most exposed to bias and regulation, because it affects who is rejected. Insist on audit results, explanations and a human decision point before rejection.

Conversational AI

Text and chat assistants that respond to applicants in seconds, ask qualifying questions and schedule interviews directly onto managers' calendars. In hourly hiring, where applicants take the first offer of an interview, this measurably raises hire rates.

Interview intelligence

Joins video calls, transcribes, writes notes structured to your scorecard and syncs them to the ATS. Also produces interviewer metrics (talk time, question consistency). Improves decision quality more than it saves time; needs candidate consent.

Scheduling automation

Less glamorous, large payoff: interviewer pools, load balancing, self-scheduling and automatic rescheduling for complex loops.

Writing and workflow assistants

Job-description drafts, outreach templates, profile summaries, candidate-facing updates. Useful, cheap, and increasingly free inside the tools you already have; rarely a reason to buy a separate product.

faq.q: Which type of recruitment AI should a small company start with?
faq.a: An AI sourcing agent if the problem is finding candidates (it replaces hours no one has), or conversational/scheduling automation if the problem is responding to too many applicants. Screening models matter most at high volume.

faq.q: Is LinkedIn Recruiter recruitment AI?
faq.a: It includes AI features (search assistance, message drafting) on top of a profile database, so it belongs in the AI talent search type. The recruiter still does the searching and messaging.

title: Where recruitment AI pays off: use cases by team
description: Concrete before-and-after scenarios for startups, agencies, high-volume employers, enterprise talent teams and job seekers.
body:
A startup with no recruiter

Before: the founder posts on two job boards, gets inbound that does not fit, and spends Sunday nights sending LinkedIn messages that go unanswered.
After: an AI sourcing agent takes a two-paragraph brief, finds and ranks several hundred relevant people, verifies emails and phone numbers, sends personalised email and SMS outreach and follow-ups, and delivers a dozen interested candidates in the first week. The founder's time goes into interviews instead of search. Cost is typically a flat team price rather than a per-recruiter licence.

A staffing agency

Before: each recruiter works four or five searches, limited by how many profiles they can read and messages they can send; InMail caps bind.
After: agents run the top-of-funnel for every open requisition in parallel over email and SMS; recruiters spend their day on calls with people who have already replied. Fill speed rises without adding seats.

A retailer hiring thousands of hourly staff

Before: applicants wait days for a response and take the first interview offered elsewhere; store managers juggle scheduling.
After: conversational AI answers every applicant within a minute by text, asks knockout questions and books an interview on the manager's calendar. Time to interview drops from days to minutes and the show rate rises.

An enterprise talent acquisition team

Before: hundreds of interviewers with inconsistent notes; sourcers spend most of their hours in Boolean search; coordinators spend theirs in calendars.
After: interview intelligence writes structured notes and flags inconsistency; AI talent search and sourcing agents cover more roles; scheduling automation handles panels. The gains are quality and coverage more than headcount reduction.

A job seeker

You will encounter recruitment AI as a chatbot, a one-way video interview with automated scoring, a matching score you never see, or a personalised email from a company you did not apply to. Knowing which is which helps: read chapter 6 on your rights and the FAQ for practical advice.

Pattern. Recruitment AI pays off fastest where a task is high volume, repetitive and currently done badly or not at all: outbound sourcing in small teams, applicant response in high-volume hiring, note-taking everywhere.

faq.q: Can recruitment AI replace a recruiter?
faq.a: It replaces parts of the job: searching, first contact, scheduling, notes. It does not replace the judgement calls, the selling of the role, the negotiation or the relationship. Teams that adopt it do more hiring per recruiter rather than hiring fewer recruiters.

faq.q: What is the typical return on an AI sourcing agent?
faq.a: The honest measure is interested replies per week per dollar compared with the alternative (a Recruiter seat plus recruiter hours, or an agency fee). Teams report the agent producing in days what a part-time sourcing effort produced in weeks; results depend heavily on the brief and the role.

title: Benefits and limits: what the evidence supports
description: Where recruitment AI demonstrably helps, where it fails, and how to tell the difference in your own numbers.
body:
Benefits with evidence behind them

  • Speed to first contact. Conversational AI and sourcing agents respond in minutes rather than days. In hourly hiring this translates directly into higher interview show rates; in passive sourcing, into reaching candidates before competitors do.
  • Coverage. Agents and AI search cover roles and candidate pools a small team could not reach, including people not on LinkedIn or not active on it.
  • Consistency. Structured notes and scorecards applied to every interview reduce the influence of memory and mood on decisions.
  • Recruiter time. The hours removed from search, scheduling and notes are real and measurable; what you do with them determines whether the business sees a return.

Limits

  • Garbage in. A vague brief produces an irrelevant shortlist, from any tool. Agents are only as good as the two paragraphs you gave them.
  • Prediction is not understanding. Matching models learn correlations in past data. If past hiring favoured one group, a model trained on it will too, unless deliberately corrected.
  • Confident errors. Language models sometimes state false facts fluently: an invented qualification in a summary, a wrong company in an email. Good products ground every claim in source data and let you check it.
  • Candidate reaction. Generic AI outreach is already being ignored; obviously automated interviews are resented. The tools that work are the ones candidates cannot tell apart from a thoughtful human, or that are honest about being automated and quick.
  • Data rights. Scraping, contact enrichment and automated decisions have legal constraints that vary by country. See chapter 6.

How to measure it yourself

Pick one metric per tool before you buy, and measure it against the status quo for four weeks:

Tool typeMetricCompare against
Sourcing agentInterested replies per week; shortlist relevance rated by the hiring managerYour recruiter's outbound, or an agency
Screening/matchingAgreement with human reviewers; adverse-impact ratio by groupCurrent manual screen
Conversational AITime to scheduled interview; show rateCurrent email/phone process
Interview intelligenceScorecard completion rate; debrief timeCurrent notes

faq.q: Does recruitment AI reduce bias or increase it?
faq.a: Either. Structured notes and consistent criteria reduce human bias; matching models trained on biased history reproduce it. The outcome depends on what the model predicts, how it is audited, and whether humans keep the decision.

faq.q: Why do candidates ignore AI outreach?
faq.a: Because most of it is template mail-merge with a first name inserted. Outreach that references the person's actual work, is short, and arrives by a channel they read (email, SMS) performs well whether a person or an agent wrote it.

title: Bias, regulation and candidate rights
description: NYC Local Law 144, the EU AI Act, GDPR automated-decision rules, US EEOC guidance and what they mean for employers and candidates.
body:
This chapter is general information, not legal advice. Rules change; check with counsel in your jurisdiction.

Why regulators care

Hiring decisions affect livelihoods, and models trained on past hiring can encode past discrimination invisibly. Regulators have responded by targeting automated decisions that affect selection, which is why screening and matching tools face more rules than outreach or note-taking tools.

The main rules

RuleWho it coversWhat it requires
New York City Local Law 144 (2023)Employers using automated employment decision tools for NYC rolesAnnual independent bias audit, public summary of results, notice to candidates, alternative process on request
EU AI Act (phased 2025–2027)Providers and deployers of AI used in recruitment and selection in the EUClassified high-risk: risk management, data governance, human oversight, transparency to candidates, logging, conformity assessment
GDPR Article 22Any processing of EU/UK residents' dataRight not to be subject to solely automated decisions with significant effects; right to explanation and human review; lawful basis for enrichment and profiling
US federal (Title VII, ADA, EEOC guidance)US employersEmployer liable for disparate impact of tools it uses, including vendor tools; accommodations for disabled candidates in AI assessments
State laws (Illinois AI Video Interview Act, Colorado AI Act, California regulations)Employers in those statesNotice and consent for AI video analysis; impact assessments; anti-discrimination duties for high-risk AI

What this means for employers

  • Keep a human decision point before any rejection influenced by a model.
  • Ask vendors for bias audit results, adverse-impact analysis and the ability to explain individual outputs.
  • Tell candidates when AI is used in assessment and offer an alternative.
  • Check the lawful basis for contact enrichment and outreach data in each country; email outreach to professionals is generally permitted on legitimate-interest grounds in many jurisdictions with opt-out, but the rules on SMS and on scraping differ.
  • Outreach, scheduling and note-taking tools carry far less regulatory exposure than screening tools; start there if risk tolerance is low.

What this means for candidates

  • In NYC and the EU you are entitled to know when an automated tool assessed you and, in the EU/UK, to request human review of a solely automated decision.
  • You can ask any employer how AI was used in your application; many will answer even where not required.
  • If a one-way video interview is scored automatically, you may be entitled to notice and, in some states, consent.
  • Personalised outreach you did not ask for is usually lawful; a reply of "please remove me" must be honoured by reputable tools.

faq.q: Does NYC Local Law 144 apply to AI sourcing tools?
faq.a: It applies to tools that substantially assist or replace discretionary decisions on hiring or promotion. Sourcing and outreach tools that find and contact candidates, leaving all selection to humans, are generally outside its core scope; screening and ranking tools used to filter applicants are inside it. Confirm with counsel for your setup.

faq.q: Is AI recruiting legal in the EU?
faq.a: Yes, but AI used for recruitment and selection is classed as high-risk under the EU AI Act, which brings documentation, oversight and transparency duties, and GDPR limits solely automated decisions. Compliance is achievable; it requires process.

title: How to evaluate a recruitment AI product
description: Twenty questions to ask a vendor, a four-week pilot design, and the red flags that should end a conversation.
body:
Twenty questions for any vendor

What it does

  1. Which specific task does the AI complete end to end? Where does a human take over?
  2. What data does it search or learn from? Is it licensed, public, or scraped?
  3. What is the model trained or tuned to predict? (For ranking: what counts as a "good" candidate?)
  4. Can it explain each individual output, in words a hiring manager would accept?
  5. Which channels does it use to contact candidates, and how is deliverability managed?

Quality and safety

  1. What is the measured reply rate / match agreement / scheduling time for customers like us?
  2. Have you run a bias audit? Can we see the summary and the methodology?
  3. How are factual errors in generated text prevented or caught?
  4. What happens when a candidate asks to be removed or asks for human review?
  5. What do candidates see? Can we read the exact messages or questions before go-live?

Data and compliance

  1. Does our data train models used for other customers? Can we opt out?
  2. Where is data stored; what are the retention and deletion rules?
  3. Which laws have you designed for (NYC LL144, EU AI Act, GDPR)? Show the documentation.
  4. Do you have SOC 2 or ISO 27001? Can we see the report?

Commercials and fit

  1. What is the pricing model: per seat, per contact, per hire, flat? What happens at twice our volume?
  2. Is there a free tier or trial where we can measure results before paying?
  3. Which ATS and calendars does it integrate with natively?
  4. How long is implementation, and who does the work?
  5. What does a customer who churned say about why?
  6. What is on the roadmap for the next two quarters, and what was shipped in the last two?

A four-week pilot

  1. Week 0: pick one metric Interested replies per week for a sourcing agent; time to scheduled interview for conversational AI; scorecard completion for interview intelligence.
  2. Week 1: baseline Measure the current process on the same roles for one week.
  3. Weeks 2–4: run the tool On two or three live roles, with the same recruiter, same brief quality.
  4. Review Compare the metric, read a sample of candidate-facing output, ask the hiring manager to rate shortlist relevance, and total the cost including recruiter time.

Red flags

  • Cannot say what the model predicts or what data it uses.
  • No way to read candidate-facing messages before they go out.
  • Claims of "bias-free" AI (no such thing; ask for audit results instead).
  • Describes LinkedIn automation as a feature; it violates LinkedIn's terms and puts your accounts at risk. Reputable sourcing agents reach candidates by email and SMS.
  • Pricing that only makes sense on a three-year contract.

faq.q: Should we pilot more than one recruitment AI tool at once?
faq.a: Pilot one tool per task type at a time, on different roles, so results are attributable. Running two sourcing agents on the same role confuses candidates and the data.

faq.q: How long before recruitment AI shows results?
faq.a: Outreach and scheduling tools show results within one to two weeks. Screening models need enough applicant volume to evaluate, usually a month or more. Interview intelligence is immediate for notes and takes a quarter to show in decision quality.

title: Implementing recruitment AI: a practical sequence
description: The order in which to introduce AI into a recruiting process, what to fix first, and how to bring hiring managers and candidates along.
body:
Fix the process before you automate it

AI amplifies whatever it is pointed at. Before any tool: write real job briefs (must-haves, nice-to-haves, compensation), define interview stages and scorecards, and make sure every candidate lives in one system. A sourcing agent given a vague brief returns vague people; interview AI applied to unstructured interviews produces well-formatted noise.

A sensible order

  1. Writing assistants Job descriptions, outreach drafts, candidate updates. Zero risk, immediate time saved, usually already in your ATS.
  2. Scheduling automation Self-scheduling and panel coordination. Low risk, visible relief for coordinators and candidates.
  3. Sourcing agents or AI talent search The biggest change in output for most teams. Start with two roles that have been open too long. Read every message the agent sends in week one; after that, sample.
  4. Interview intelligence Introduce with consent language and a clear statement that recordings are for notes, not evaluation. Share the notes with interviewers so they see the benefit.
  5. Conversational AI For high-volume hiring, once the application flow and knockout criteria are agreed with operations.
  6. Screening and matching Last, because it is the most regulated and the most consequential. Run it in shadow mode (scores visible, not acted on) and audit for adverse impact before letting it influence rejections.

People

  • Recruiters fear replacement; show them the hours returned and give them the judgement work. Make one recruiter the owner of each tool.
  • Hiring managers care about shortlist quality and speed. Ask them to rate shortlists; use the ratings to tune briefs.
  • Candidates accept AI that is fast, honest and reversible. Always offer a human route.
  • Legal and security need the vendor documentation from chapter 7 early, not at signature.

Budget

For a team of fewer than ten recruiters: writing and scheduling features are usually free inside the ATS; a sourcing agent costs a flat team price, usually quoted rather than listed; interview intelligence is priced per interviewer in the low hundreds per month. Conversational and screening platforms are enterprise purchases.

faq.q: Should we buy one AI recruiting platform or several tools?
faq.a: Several narrow tools that integrate with your ATS usually beat one platform, because the best sourcing agent, the best scheduler and the best screening model come from different vendors. Consolidate later if integration costs bite.

faq.q: How do we announce recruitment AI to candidates?
faq.a: Plainly: a short line on the careers page and in relevant messages saying which steps use AI, that a human reviews decisions, and how to request an alternative. Candidates object to concealment more than to AI.

title: Where recruitment AI is going
description: Agents that run whole requisitions, candidate-side AI, the end of Boolean, and what will not change.
body:
From features to agents

The first wave of recruitment AI added features to existing tools: a better search box, a drafted email. The current wave replaces whole workflows with agents: brief in, shortlist and replies out. The next step is agents that own a requisition end to end: sourcing, screening against structured criteria, scheduling and candidate communication, with a recruiter supervising several at once. The sourcing half of that already exists.

Candidate-side AI

Candidates now use AI to write applications, prepare for interviews and, increasingly, to apply at scale. Application volume is rising and signal per application is falling. Expect employers to respond by relying less on inbound applications and more on outbound sourcing and verified skills, and by moving assessment to live, structured conversations that are hard to automate from the candidate side.

The end of Boolean and of the seat

Semantic search has already made Boolean strings optional. Pricing is following the work: from per-recruiter seats towards per-team or per-outcome pricing, because an agent's output does not scale with the number of humans logged in.

Regulation will shape product design

The EU AI Act's requirements for logging, explanation and human oversight are becoming default features globally, because vendors build once. Expect every serious screening and ranking product to ship audit reports and explanation views as standard.

What will not change

  • People take jobs from people. The conversation that closes a candidate stays human.
  • A clear brief beats a clever model.
  • Candidates remember how they were treated, whoever (or whatever) sent the message.

faq.q: Will AI recruiters replace human recruiters?
faq.a: The sourcing, scheduling and administrative parts of recruiting are being automated quickly. The parts that involve persuasion, judgement, negotiation and trust are not. The job is shifting towards those parts, with each recruiter supported by agents doing the volume work.

faq.q: How should job seekers prepare for AI-driven hiring?
faq.a: Keep a complete, accurate public profile and a reachable email, because outbound sourcing is growing; expect skills-based and structured interviews that reward specifics; and reply to personalised outreach, which increasingly comes from agents on behalf of real teams.

title: How AI candidate screening works, and where it fails
description: What happens between an application arriving and a shortlist appearing: parsing, knockout rules, matching, criteria-based ranking, and the four places the process breaks.
body:
AI candidate screening is the use of software to read applications and decide which ones a human should look at. It is the oldest and most widely deployed form of recruitment AI, it is the one most candidates will meet, and it is the one regulators have written the most rules about. This chapter follows an application from the moment it arrives to the moment it appears, or does not appear, on a shortlist, and names the four places where the process goes wrong.

Why screening became the first thing to automate

A posted role at a recognisable company draws several hundred applications; popular remote roles draw thousands. Reading each one for two minutes is a full working week per role, which nobody has. So recruiters developed shortcuts: scan the current title, the last employer and the first education line, then decide. Screening software started as an attempt to make that shortcut consistent, and it inherited the shortcut's blind spots. The rise of AI-written applications has sharpened the problem: when every CV reads well, the surface signals a human skims for stop meaning anything.

The five steps, in order

1. Parsing

The application (a CV, a form, a LinkedIn import) is converted into fields: names, dates, employers, titles, skills, qualifications, locations. Parsers have improved sharply since language models replaced rule-based extraction, but they still misread unusual layouts, two-column designs, and careers that do not follow a title-employer-date pattern. Anything the parser drops is invisible to every later step.

2. Knockout rules

Before any ranking, most systems apply hard filters the employer set: work authorisation, a required licence, a location radius, a minimum years-of-experience figure. These are the cheapest step and the most dangerous, because a badly specified rule rejects silently and at scale. A minimum-years rule written as a proxy for seniority will exclude career changers who are stronger than the people it keeps.

3. Matching

The parsed application is compared with the role. Older systems count keyword overlap. Current systems use the embedding approach described in chapter 2: role and candidate are each turned into a vector and the distance between them is the match. Embeddings understand that revenue operations and sales ops are close and that a Django developer can probably learn Flask, which keyword systems cannot. They do not understand whether the person was any good at either.

4. Ranking against criteria

The better systems go beyond a single similarity score and evaluate each applicant against the criteria the hiring team actually wrote down: the must-haves, the preferences, the disqualifiers. A language model reads the application against each criterion and records whether it is met, partly met, not met or not evidenced, with a short reason. The output is a structured assessment rather than a number, which is what makes it auditable. Products such as Noon's inbound screening work this way: applicants are evaluated against the role's criteria and non-negotiables, hiring-manager feedback adjusts the weighting per role, and the advance or reject decision is written back to the ATS stage.

5. The decision and the hand-off

Finally the system does something with the result: tags the application, moves it to a stage, sends a rejection, or queues it for a human. This is where the legal character of the tool is decided. A system that recommends and leaves the move to a recruiter is treated differently from one that rejects automatically, and the difference is often a single setting.

What the system is actually predicting

Every screening model is a prediction machine, and the question to ask any vendor is a prediction of what? There are three honest answers and one dishonest one.

TargetHow it is trainedWhat can go wrong
Similarity to the role descriptionNo training on your data; compares textRewards people who write like the job ad, including with AI
Fit against stated criteriaCriteria written per role, model reads evidenceOnly as good as the criteria; vague must-haves produce vague assessments
Likelihood of being hiredTrained on past hiring decisionsReproduces whatever past decisions favoured, including bias
Likelihood of success in the jobNeeds performance data most companies do not haveUsually a marketing claim; ask to see the outcome data

The third target is the one that produced the well-known failures: a model trained on a decade of hires learns the decade's preferences. Most current vendors have moved to the first two targets precisely because they do not require historical hiring data, but it is still worth asking.

Four places it fails

  • The parser dropped it. Non-standard careers, scanned documents, and portfolios are under-read. Ask for the parse rate and what happens to applications the parser is unsure about.
  • The rule was a proxy. Years of experience, degree requirements and continuous-employment filters stand in for qualities they correlate with weakly. The Harvard Business School Hidden Workers study found most employers acknowledged their filters reject qualified people.
  • The text was the candidate. Similarity scoring cannot tell a strong engineer with a terse CV from a weak one with a polished, AI-written one. Fraudulent and duplicated applications, now common in remote roles, pass this step easily; detecting them is a separate job, covered by dedicated fraud-detection tools rather than by the screener.
  • Nobody looked at the rejects. If the tool rejects automatically and no one samples the rejected pile, systematic errors persist for months. The simplest control is a weekly review of twenty random rejections.

The rules that apply

Screening is the recruitment AI use case regulators have addressed most directly. New York City's Local Law 144 requires an annual bias audit and candidate notice before an automated employment decision tool is used to screen; the EU AI Act classes recruitment screening as high-risk, with documentation, human-oversight and transparency duties; and under GDPR a candidate can object to a decision made solely by automated means. In the United States the EEOC has made clear that an employer is responsible for disparate impact produced by a vendor's tool. Chapter 6 covers these in detail; the practical consequence is that the screener should recommend, a human should decide, and the adverse-impact ratio by group should be measured, not assumed.

What good looks like

A well-run screening setup has written criteria per role, agreed with the hiring manager before the post goes live; knockout rules limited to genuine legal or logistical requirements; an assessment per applicant that cites evidence from the application rather than a bare score; a human making the final reject on anyone the model was unsure about; and a monthly check of agreement between the model and a human reviewer on a sample, alongside the adverse-impact ratio. The vendor questions in chapter 7 apply; the two that matter most here are what does the model predict and can I see why it rejected this person.

Further reading: the glossary entry; Noon's plain-language explainer on what AI resume screening is; and the EEOC technical assistance on adverse impact in algorithmic tools.

faq.q: Does AI screening read every application?
faq.a: Yes, which is its main advantage over a human skim. Whether it reads them well depends on the parser and on how specific the role criteria are. Ask what happens to applications the parser cannot read confidently.

faq.q: Can a candidate beat AI screening by stuffing keywords?
faq.a: Against keyword-matching systems, partly. Against criteria-based assessment, far less: the model looks for evidence that a criterion is met, and a list of skills with no supporting experience is recorded as not evidenced. Writing a plain, specific account of what you did is the reliable approach.

faq.q: Is it legal to reject applicants automatically?
faq.a: In most places yes, with conditions: New York City requires a bias audit and notice, the EU AI Act imposes human-oversight duties, and GDPR gives candidates the right to object to solely automated decisions. Many employers configure the tool to recommend and keep the reject decision with a recruiter to stay clear of these thresholds.
